n: Verses 1–12 sketch the fool. Honor fits a fool about as well as snow in summer or rain at harvest—out of place and even harmful.

f.w: rain in harvest
f.g: Rare in Israel’s dry summer and damaging to ripe grain.

f.w: seemly
f.g: seemly = fitting.

n: An undeserved curse is like a darting bird or swallow—it flutters about but never lands. Unjust curses have no power.

f.w: the curse causeless shall not come

n: A whip for the horse, a bridle for the donkey, and a rod for the fool—some only respond to force.

f.w: a rod for the fool's back

n: Don’t answer a fool on his own terms, or you’ll become just like him.

f.w: Answer not a fool according to his folly
f.g: Don’t sink to his level.

n: Yet sometimes you must answer a fool, or he’ll think he’s wise. Verses 4–5 placed side by side teach that wisdom knows when to answer and when to stay silent.

f.w: Answer a fool according to his folly
f.g: Expose his folly so he won’t be wise in his own eyes.

f.w: conceit
f.g: conceit = opinion, estimation.

n: Sending a message by a fool is like cutting off your own feet or drinking poison—you only hurt yourself.

f.w: drinketh damage
f.g: Drinks down violence—brings harm on himself.

n: A proverb in a fool’s mouth is as useless as a lame man’s legs.

f.w: The legs of the lame are not equal
f.g: Or “hang limp,” useless.

n: Honoring a fool is like tying a stone into a sling—it won’t work and may backfire.

f.w: bindeth a stone in a sling
f.g: A stone tied in can’t be thrown; or it whips back and hurts the slinger.

n: A proverb in a fool’s mouth is like a thorn in a drunk’s hand—he doesn’t know how to use it and may hurt others.

f.w: a thorn goeth up into the hand of a drunkard
f.g: A drunk waving a thornbush, harming himself and others.

n: A difficult verse with many readings. KJV: God, who made all, repays fools and sinners. Many modern versions: like an archer wounding at random is one who hires a fool or a passer-by.

f.w: The great God that formed all things
f.g: The Hebrew is uncertain; it may mean “a master craftsman” or “an archer.”

n: A fool returns to his folly like a dog returns to its vomit. Peter quotes this about those who go back to sins they had left.

f.w: As a dog returneth to his vomit

n: There’s more hope for a fool than for someone who thinks he’s already wise. Pride is harder to fix than ignorance.

f.w: wise in his own conceit

n: Verses 13–16 sketch the lazy person. His excuse: “There’s a lion in the road!”

f.w: There is a lion in the way

n: A comic picture: the lazy person turns on his bed like a door on its hinges—moving, but going nowhere.

f.w: As the door turneth upon his hinges
f.g: Lots of motion, no progress.

n: He buries his hand in the dish and is too tired to bring it back to his mouth. (See 19:24.)

f.w: it grieveth him
f.g: It wears him out.

f.w: hideth his hand in his bosom
f.g: Better “buries his hand in the dish.”

n: The lazy person thinks he is wiser than seven people who can give sensible answers. Laziness often hides behind excuses that sound clever.

f.w: seven men that can render a reason
f.g: Seven = many; people who answer with good sense.

n: Meddling in someone else’s quarrel is like grabbing a stray dog by the ears—you’re asking to get bitten.

f.w: taketh a dog by the ears
f.g: Dogs were often wild scavengers, not pets.

n: Like a madman shooting flaming arrows and deadly darts…

f.w: firebrands
f.g: firebrands = flaming arrows or burning sticks.

n: …so is someone who deceives his neighbor and then says, “I was only joking!” Harmful “jokes” do real damage.

f.w: Am not I in sport?
f.g: “Wasn’t I just kidding?”

n: Without wood a fire goes out; without gossip, quarrels die down.

f.w: talebearer
f.g: talebearer = gossip, whisperer.

n: As charcoal feeds embers and wood feeds fire, a quarrelsome person fuels conflict.

f.w: a contentious man to kindle strife

n: Gossip is like delicious morsels that sink deep inside. (Repeats 18:8.)

f.w: as wounds
f.g: Likely “like delicious morsels.”

n: Smooth, fervent words hiding an evil heart are like a cheap clay pot coated with glaze—shiny outside, worthless inside.

f.w: a potsherd covered with silver dross
f.g: A clay pot coated with glaze or cheap silver slag.

f.w: Burning lips
f.g: Fervent, warm-sounding words.

n: A hateful person disguises it with his words while storing up deceit inside.

f.w: dissembleth
f.g: dissembleth = disguises, pretends.

n: When he speaks graciously, don’t trust him—his heart is full of evil.

f.w: seven abominations
f.g: Seven = completeness; his heart is full of evil.

n: His hatred may be hidden by deceit, but his wickedness will be exposed publicly.

f.w: his wickedness shall be shewed

n: Whoever digs a pit for others will fall into it; whoever rolls a stone will have it roll back on him.

f.w: Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein

n: A liar hates those he hurts, and flattery leads to ruin.

f.w: a flattering mouth worketh ruin
